The House resumed from Tuesday, March 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. 78, respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company.

Georgian Bay Canal Company

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
At
nine o'clock on Tuesday evening I had practically concluded my remarks on this bill, but I shall take this opportunity again to make plain, my position as I am anxious not to be misunderstood in the matter. It is not my intention to prevent the bill from being referred to and considered by the committee on railways. Unfortunately, under the rules of the House, I have been obliged to extend my remarks over three different evenings; but it will be found that altogether I have spoken for less than an hour. It cannot be said therefore that I have in any way endeavoured to talk the bill out.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Some hon. gentlemen over the way laugh at this but they speak sometimes for two hours. I do not inflict my remarks on this House very frequently and, I repeat, I have no desire whatever to try and talk this bill out. I thought it best to discuss ithe bill on the second reading inasmuch as it is one of great interest to the public of Ontario and Quebec although it appears nominally on the list of private bills.
As I pointed out before, I want to have hon. members as fully informed as possible of the facts regarding this bill before it goes to the committee, where I hope it will be very thoroughly considered. I am not opposed to the building of the Georgian Bay canal. Indeed, I would favour the project if it were carried out on its own merits. I do not think, however, that it should be financed from the profits of power development at the expense of the power users of Quebec and Ontario, nor do I think that the immense power possibilities of the Ottawa river should be tied up in any way to a private company.
We may as well face the facts of this situation. The Dominion and each of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario have certain rights regarding the Ottawa river. My impression is that no one knows exactly what their respective rights are, but I do not intend to discuss that phase of the matter. As they each have rights, however, the only sensible thing for them to do would be to meet around a table with a view to finding some reasonable and satisfactory way of dealing with the problem. That is what individuals would do under similar conditions. Even if the Georgian Bay canal charter were renewed, that company could do nothing in the way of distributing power in either Quebec or Ontario until they made arrangements with the provinces. All this being so, I urge that the Dominion government take over the enterprise under the powers given them by section 5 of
chapter 128 of the statutes of 1906, which I read into Hansard last Tuesday evening. Such action would not hurt the shareholders of the present company as they would be recompensed1 for their expenditure, while it would place the whole problem in such a position that it could be dealt with on a common sense basis by the Dominion and the two provinces, in the best interests of all concerned.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that after all, whether we are members of provincial legislatures or of this House we represent the people of Canada and should do our best to see that these great properties are used entirely in the public interest. By retaining possession of and developing these water-powers the three governments, the Dominion government and those of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, will not only be receiving a large annual revenue but will be ensuring for all time a supply of electricity for light, heat and power at a reasonable rate for the people of these provinces.

speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman resumes his seat I would like to ask him, just for information, how it is proposed to separate the development of the water-power and the construction and operation of the canal, having in view the paramount need of navigable waters?

there is any great difficulty about that. If the representatives of these three governments will meet together at a common table they will find a way to solve that difficulty.

M'r. CANNON: You are very frank about it, anyway.

Georgian Bay Canal Company

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I always believe in being
frank. I am not killing time, because I have some facts to present, but the reason I am going to carry on until nine o'clock is because this is too important a question to decide in fifteen or twenty minutes, as might have been the case this evening.
I was not in the House either of the other evenings when this question came up. I come from a part of the country, like my good friend from Nipissing, which is vitally interested in the question of water routes, but while I have a great deal of sympathy for any attitude he may take I will likely disagree with him ultimately. I must look at it from my own standpoint, and I can look back well over twenty years during which the Georgian Bay canal question was being discussed in my section of the country, upon this very charter which we are discussing tonight. That charter was granted in 1894, thirty-three years ago; not before I was born, I will admit, but back in that direction. Though it was granted so long ago, I made it my business to look up the original charter, and I find that those originally named in it are almost all dead, but the charter is still alive, gasping for breath it is true, but still gapping.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Going strong.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Possibly. I am not going to argue too strongly against it to-night, but I am going to show, until nine o'clock, some of the reasons why I think the charter should have been allowed to expire with a lot of the original charter holders, and probably I will continue on Monday and give some others.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Who were originally
named?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
There are too many (to read, but most of them are dead. I have not had time to-night to look through the list, and there are no doubt a few of them still living, but I believe the greater majority have passed away. This charter was then carried on by Sir Robert Perks for many years; then he got tired of it and handed it over to other interests.
In all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, and not particularly speaking of this charter at ah, when I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) objecting to a charter to-night, one with which I was not familiar at all, I found myself more or less in agreement with his remarks when he said that we are, or certainly in the past have been, too prone to grant charters for all kinds

of projects. I made it my business to glance through the volume of 1894, and I found many charters are not alive now, charters which had been renewed many times but which were finally allowed to expire quietly. I should say that more than half and probably two-thirds of this list of 1894 were charters which never served any useful purpose at all, and many of them were grabbed off for the purpose of holding up some legitimate progress. They were secured in order that those who got them might take some group of men by the neck and say, "You cannot do this because we secured the charter first, and you must pay us before you can go on."
Mr. LAPIERRE; They were granted under Conservative governments.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
That was true in 1894,
but I can tell my friend that this has been going on since 1896 as well, and even all through the ten years that I have been here. I can frankly say that no matter whether it was a Liberal government, a Unionist government, or a Conservative government, much the same process has been carried out; and I have come to the conclusion that unless there is really some good reason for charters to be granted it is time to call a halt to a great many of these applications.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? If such is the case, why not allow it to go to committee before further discussion, to see whetner those asking for the renewal can give some good reason for their request?

The principle of granting this charter; that is the principle we are discussing to-night and that is what I am speaking of. Until we decide that the principle of granting this charter is good, it is our duty to discuss it and come to some decision in this House.
Before my good friend, the Hon. the Speaker, tells me it is nine o'clock, may I point out that the premier of Ontario has come out flatly against this renewal. Prophecies are very dangerous things for politicians to make, especially before elections, I know, but I am going to make a prophecy

The House resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 61, to amend the Soldier Settlement Act, 1919-Hon. Mr. Forke-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Revaluation of land sold to settlers.

When the committee rose,
Mr. Chairman, we were discussing the matter of appeal, and I would like to say a few words in regard to that aspect of the bill. Part of this section reads as follows:

and if any applicant is dissatisfied with the decision of the board he may, within such time as is prescribed by regulations made by the Governor in Council, appeal to the Exchequer court of Canada and the decision of that court shall be final.
There seems to be a good deal of objection to an appeal to the Exchequer court. Some seem to think that this would be expensive; that it would entail quite a long delay, and in fact that it would be altogether too cumbersome a procedure for the soldier settler. It may, however, not be so cumbersome or difficult as it appears on the surface. Section 42 of the Exchequer Court Act, chapter 140 of the Statutes of Canada reads:
The court may, for the purpose of taking account or making enquiries, or for the determination of any question or issue of fact, refer any cause, claim, matter or petition to the Registrar or any other officer of the court, or to any official or special referee for inquiry and report, and may also, if it thinks it expedient so to do, call in the aid of one or more assessors specially qualified, and try and hear such cause, matter or petition, wholly or partially, with the assistance of such assessor or assessors.
In a case of appeal I suppose the procedure would be this: An appeal would be made to the Exchequer court, which would nominate some individual, probably the county court judge in the district from which the appeal was made. He would make an investigation and report to the Exchequer court which
would then render a final decision. I am not sufficiently acquainted with all the procedure, but I know of certain cases where individual matters have been referred to the Exchequer court and where they have been settled quickly and decisively, without delay. What may take place as regards many appeals I am not in a position to say. Some of the lawyers in the House will be better acquainted with that phase of the matter than I am.
I do not believe there are going to be as many appeals as some members seem to think.
I believe there are more satisfied soldier settlers than we commonly imagine. I have been in the department only for three or four months, and I have signed quite a number of transfers of land where the people buying soldier settler lands have been paying higher prices than the soldier settlers originally paid for them when they purchased them from the Soldier Settlement Board. That shows that a number of these lots, if they were put in the market now, would be worth more money than the soldier settlers paid for them originally.
Does that take into account any improvements such as the soldier settler makes on the land?

I am not in a position to
say. Generally when cases come before me, the price at which the land was originally sold to the settler and the price offered for it at the present time are stated; I am advised by the Soldier Settlement Board that this is a fair value for the land, and the transfer is usually made. I do not want the impression to go abroad that this is taking place in many cases because it is only in a few cases that it occurs. I cite this only to show that land was not sold at too high a price to commence with. I am pretty well acquainted with the position in which soldier settlers find themselves having lived all these years in western Canada, and I am just as anxious as any other hon. member to help them. I know many of them find themselves in impossible positions, and something must be done if they are to be put on their feet and enabled to carry on successfully.
Many seem to think the money the Dominion government has spent in connection with soldier land settlement has all been lost. That is not the case. They have cultivated a great deal of land; they have produced a great deal of wealth, and many other things can be put to the credit of the work of the soldier settlers. I have mentioned just how I think an appeal to the Exchequer court
Soldier Settlement Act

will work out, but I will welcome any suggestions along this line in order that the legislation may be improved.
I have a suggestion to make, showing how an appeal can be made in another way. I will read the clause and then the committee can draw their own conclusions. The clause I would suggest, dealing with the value of the land, reads:
Upon the receipt of an application made in accordance with the terms of this section the board shall ascertain and determine the depreciation in value as set forth in paragraph (c) of this section; and if any applicant is dissatisfied with the decision of the board he may, within such time as is prescribed by regulations made by the Governor in Council, appeal said decision by notice in writing to the board who shall thereupon refer the appeal for final decision to district or county court judge of the judicial district or county in which the land is situate or in the province of Quebec to the judge of the Superior court having jurisdiction in the district in which the land is situate, and such judge shall fix a convenient time and place for hearing and determining such appeal.
Is that a proposed amendment?

I am putting it before the committee as a suggestion to think over, not as an amendment. I may say that in introducing this bill I am not wedded to any particular section.	If the committee can
suggest improvements I am quite willing to listen and to take the decision of the committee on the matter. It is simply an appeal to the county court judge.
Alone?
Alone, of course with a hearing given to the board and to the soldier settler himself or his representative.
What wi'l that cost the soldier settler, or will there be any cost to him?
The bill will cover that. By regulation of the Governor in Council it could be made so that it will not cost the soldier anything, or otherwise.
What regulation has the minister in mind?

It says:
Expenditures necessarily incurred by or in connection with the administration of this act as may be provided by regulation, shall be paid out of monies appropriated from time to time by parliament to soldier land settlement.

Does that apply to the
expenses of the soldiers or the expenses of the department?

I think it is intended to
cover both.

The amendment which the minister has just read, it seems to me, would be much more preferable, so far as Alberta at least is concerned, than the section as it now stands. During the last few years, because of the conditions prevailing, largely due to deflation, our district court judges had a good deal of experience in the matter of land values. There have been many applications before the district courts for mortgage foreclosures, and by reason of that fact the district court judges know land values fairly well in their own particular district. I am satisfied that the returned men, in view of the fact that the court is right in their midst, would be better satisfied with judgments from that court than from anyone appointed by the Exchequer court for that purpose. If the minister could see his way clear to move that amendment, I think it would be in the best interests of all concerned. We should try and set up machinery that will be satisfactory to the returned men in order that we may get this situation eventually cleaned up.
The hon. member for New Westminster this afternoon brought before the committee resolutions passed by a certain organization asking for a flat reduction of twenty-five per cent, or something of that nature, on all outstanding accounts of the soldier settlers. I know something about this situation so far as Alberta is concerned, and I would emphasize very strongly that a flat rate reduction would not be acceptable in our province because of the injustices that would be created, and that would have to be met later on. In my own district, for instance, no doubt some soldier settlers bought at the right price and are to-day well satisfied with their bargain. Why should we give them a flat reduction of twenty-five per cent? They have received good value for the money they have expended on these properties. On the other hand, there are many properties that would not be satisfactory to the returned men even if you give this flat reduction of twenty-five per cent. In fact it would only keep the settler there a short time, and eventually he would leave the farm because the twenty-five per cent flat reduction would not be sufficint to meet his particular case. Under these circumstances I hope the minister will not consider any proposal for a flat rate reduction on all these properties. Let us have a proper valuation as set out in this legislation, together with the amendment put before the committee a few minutes ago by the minister, and then I think we shall settle this question in a very short time to the satisfaction both of the returned men and the people of Canada.

Soldier Settlement Act

I came
down this evening, Mr. Chairman, with the intention of making a suggestion in regard to this particular section and asking the minister to endorse it. I felt disposed, if the government wanted the Exchequer court of Canada to pass final judgment on any appeal, to suggest to them the advisability of the appeal being made to the county judge, who would hear the evidence and make his report to the Exchequer court, whose decision would be final. I think the sending of

individual may be a gentleman who was doing business in that particular community, and may give a special favour to the soldier. I wish to throw out one
or two suggestions for the consideration of the committee. I am delighted to see that there is a desire on both sides of the House to make this bill as beneficial to the soldiers as possible. There are two principles we should keep firmly fixed in mind. First, if there is to be a right of appeal given to the solider settler, then that appeal should foe as accessible as possible to him, and the procedure set up for appeal should be made as simple as possible. The second principle that I think we should keep in mind is that the revaluation which is proposed in this bill should not entail on the soldier settler a single cent in the way of cost to himself. We are fairly generally agreed that the provisions contained in this present bill providing for an appeal to the Exchequer court of Canada will not be looked upon favourably by the soldier settlers of this country. I hope that, when an application is made by the soldier settler to the Soldier Settlement Board, the board will appreciate the spirit of this act and be generous in any attitude they adopt towards the settler. I hope that a policy of that sort will be impressed upon the various supervisors in soldier settlement districts throughout Canada. If such a policy is adopted by the various boards, the number of appeals will not be as large as we are sometimes led to believe they will be. But there will undoubtedly be appeals, and the simplest and least expensive form of appeal should be established by this act.
Various suggestions in this behalf have been made by soldier organizations and by speakers on both sides of the House. It has been suggested that instead of providing for an appeal to the Exchequer court of Canada, we [DOT]should provide for an appeal to the county or district court judge of the county or district in which the land is situate, or, in the province of Quebec, where there are no county or district court judges, that the corresponding judge should be charged with the duties of hearing appeals. With regard to that suggestion, I know something of the work of the county court judges in the province of Manitoba, and
	-
I can say that at present their energies are very severely taxed. I do not know what the situation is in other provinces but I do know it to be a fact in the case of the county court judges of Manitoba that they are overworked and if this additional burden is placed upon them I think it only fair that they should be remunerated for it.
There is another objection to entrusting appeals to the county court or district court judges. The judge in question will hear the case and will dispose of it according to the ordinary rules of law, will Observe the ordinary rules of evidence, and the soldier settler, in order to get his case fairfy before that court, will be called upon to employ counsel. There is that objection, I think, to the suggestion that the appeal should lie to county or district court judges. If that scheme of appeal is adopted I think it should be provided that any legal costs incurred by the soldier settler in placing his case before the appellate court constituted by this act should be met by the Dominion of Canada, thereby observing the second principle which I enunciated at the beginning, that the revaluation should not cost the settler one cent.

If that has not been
clearly stated it should be definitely set out and provided for in the act-that there should be no cost whatever to the soldier settler in getting a fair revaluation of his land.
A further suggestion has been made that an arbitration board should be set up to hear appeals, this board to consist of three persons, one to foe the county or district court judge, or the corresponding judge in the province of Quebec, and the other two to be representatives of the Soldier Settlement Board and the soldier settler respectively. That, I think, is preferable to constituting a judge as the sole person to dispose of the appeal. But that suggestion is also open to the objection which I mentioned when speaking of the county and district court judges. If it is true that these judges are overloaded with work, as I believe them to be in Manitoba, then if they have to hear a large number of appeals it will take too long to get the revaluations completed.
Still another suggestion has been made, namely, that an arbitration board should be set up consisting of a representative of the Soldier Settlement Board in the district involved and a representative of the soldier settler himself, and that these two should

agree upon the third member. In a number of cases they would probably so agree, and that would take a good deal of work off the shoulders of the judges and, in my opinion, would expedite the work of revaluation. As I say, I have the greatest respeet for the county court judge in my district, whom I consider a personal friend; but when it comes to having him deal exclusively with the determination of land values I certainly think his judgment would be better if he had the advice of a practical farmer. I understand that my hon. friend wants the board composed of the county court judge acting as referee, together with representatives of the soldiers and the Soldier Settlement Board respectively. Those two representatives would act virtually as counsel for the two opposing parties. It is well known that in arbitrations eadh party selects its own arbitrator and in some way the third man is selected, either by the courts or by agreement between the other two. multiplying officials and making a big thing of it to have a board of three instead of simply allowing the two representatives to argue the matter out and leave the decision to the referee.

speechtext: That is offensive.

The Solicitor General says

returned man, and if he has to pay his own counsel to represent him there will not be very many soldiers who will submit cases for arbitration, for the simple reason that they will not have the money to employ counsel. If we are to deny the returned soldier the right of representation by counsel-and that is what is being done here-he will certainly not get full justice. The Minister of Justice knows only too well-he knows it probably better 
than any other man in this House-that it is the height of folly for any man to be his own advocate in any case that is submitted to a tribunal for adjudication. It is written in history, as clearly as it can be written, that the man who attempts to be his own advocate, be he lawyer or layman, is unwise and knows not how to go about securing justice. The Solicitor General declares that we want to save money. I agree with him in that regard and that is why I endorsed the suggestion put forward by the minister to-night, that there should be one county judge, a trained man well versed in the administration of the law, to adjudicate upon the facts in any case requiring his judgment. If you are really thinking of the interests of the soldier, it is far better to have his counsel appear independently before the court than to have him sit on the court itself; for a man cannot be a member of a tribunal and act as advocate for one of the parties at the same time. That is contrary to all the principles of justice. The Solicitor General, I am sure, knows that perfectly well. If you have a court of appeal of five, you cannot have one of those judges, while sitting on the court, act as advocate in behalf of one of the litigants or one of the parties who have submitted the matter which is being adjudicated upon. If therefore we deny him that representation we shall ertainly not do him full justice. I repeat, if we are going to pay the members of the arbitration board it will be far better to let one man, the county court judge, render the decision and pay counsel to represent the soldier interested.

that the establishment of the Exchequer court as an appeal tribunal was undesirable because of the fact, in the first place, that the court appears to be so far removed from the soldier and he is always faced with the delay and inconvenience which would attend an application to that court. After the time that was taken up in committee on the resolution covering this bill, over the word "diminution" as it occurs in the second line of this paragraph, the minister, if he is bound to get this bill through to-night-and it is not usual to compel the House to sit so late on a Friday- will surely be good! enough to move the amendment which I know he has in his desk and which must be something more sensible than this. If any legal gentleman in the House can explain to those of us who are not members of the legal fraternity just how there can be any diminution in the present value of land, we would like to hear the explanation.
Soldier Settlement Act

I have a long brief on
this word from a very eminent authority. I am not going to give the authority, but his conclusion is that it is a perfectly correct clause. I did not mean any disrespect to the committee in not considering an amendment. I am only repeating what I have said, namely, that I have been assured by eminent authorities that this is quite all right. I am sure every hon. member knows exactly what the clause means.

It will
probably be all right if we can keep the lawyers out of it.

This may carry, but I think if it does this committee will not be using as good judgment as it generally does. It was the considered opinion of the committee when the resolution was before it that this wording was not correct. There is no doubt that the committee would have accepted an amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar), had not a point of order been raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie). The minister himself was quite convinced on that occasion that the wording as given in the bill was not right. Surely if we are going to spend all day on this bill, we might make this clause read so that it will be intelligible, let us say, to the soldier settlers. I am sure that many of them will read this and say: There is no diminution in the present value of my land; it is worth just what it is worth; I cannot find any diminution. Would it not be better to use plain English that will be understood?

It says that it shall be the
diminution in the present value as compared with the price at which the land was bought.

It reads:
The depreciation in value to be determined shall be the diminution, not due to neglect or mismanagement on the part of the settler, in the present value of the land and the improvements sold to the settler, as compared with the price at which the settler agreed to purchase the said land and improvements from the board.
I do not see much difficulty about that.

But the diminution is not in the present value. It is the diminution from the price at which he bought the land. We are taking it for granted that there is a depreciation, and that depreciation or diminution is in the value of the land when he bought it, not in the present value.

If we said "shown in the present value," I think that would remove the difficulty.
[ Mr. Coote.]

It says, "diminution in
the present value of the land and improvements sold to the settler." There is no comma after the word "land." Why stop there? The comma is after the noun "settler." If you substitute for the words "as compared with" in line 34, paragraph c, the word "and" making it read "and the price at which the settler agreed to purchase the said land and improvements from the board,''" the meaning is still more clearly expressed. But there is no ambiguity in the clause as it stands. The discussion from time to time in the House would lead to the conclusion that some hon. members think the paragraph in question about as plain as mud.

The difficulty seems to be over this word diminution, which some of us do not know how to pronounce. The meaning of the word is, I think, a lessening or a decreasing. We can avoid all the ambiguity of this section by changing one word of two letters in the thirty-second line, the word "in" to "to". Then it would read "diminution to the present value."
The minister has a perfectly good amendment on his desk, and I think he should at least suggest it to the committee for consideration.

I am not going to move it,
but I will give it to the committee for consideration, because I am no longer sure of the English language.
Give us Scotch. We will understand it better.

I could use Scotch all right. It reads:
The depreciation in value to be determined shall be the amount by which through no neglect or mismanagement on the part of the settler the price at which the board agreed to sell the land and improvements to the settler exceeds the amount representing the present value of the said land and improvements.
If that is satisfactory to the committee, I will move it.
That is all right.

I move the amendment
accordingly, Mr. Chairman.

Amendment agreed to.

Paragraph (f) agreed to.

On the preamble.

I have
listened to the discussion very attentively, but there is one point that has not been emphasized, although it was referred to by the member for Comox-Alberni. Is there any provision in this act whereby a soldier settler can be taken from land that is of no value and put on a farm where he will have some chance of making good?
The board has actually been doing that in the past, and the passing of this act will make it much easier.

Is it the intention of
the government to supply the board with sufficient funds to allow them to do that kind of thing? It is a question simply of money; the legislation is there.
There has been no provision that I know of in that regard.

Will the government
make such provision?

That is a matter for the
government to consider.
Is there a provision in the act which allows the board to transfer a man from land that is of no value to another farm?
I could not answer that with any degree of assurance, but they have been doing that.

This is a matter of interest to the soldier settlers. I had a letter the other day inquiring about this very thing, and I just wanted to know from the minister if it is legal for the board to make such a transfer, or does the 'board do it just out of the goodness of its heart? What is the procedure?

I know that the Dominion government has been in negotiation with the provincial governments in some cases to move not only soldier settlers but other settlers away from lands on which they were not able to make a living owing to their poor quality. But a difficulty arises. The province is quite willing to move a settler from one section
to another within the province, but none of the provinces is very anxious to make any move to assist the Dominion government in moving a settler from one province to another. Hon. members will understand that between the Great lakes and Manitoba there is some very poor land and there are some very bad conditions, and the Soldier Settlement Board has assisted settlers to move to other lands in Saskatchewan to which they could be moved, but there is no regulation under which the expenses of that removal could be paid by the Dominion government.
I do not think the Soldier Settlement Board have gone into that business, though they have been moving settlers from one place to another as a matter of accommodation where they had land available.

Did the government pay
the expenses of moving.
I do not think so.

I do not think the minister has answered the question put by the hon. member for Nelson. The Soldier Settlement Board does not move ordinary settlers from one district to another. That has come under the jurisdiction of the federal government, the provinces and the railways. We have soldier settlers on lands that have no agricultural value. I am quite aware that the board may have in its possession lands to which these men could be transferred. I understand the legislation in force at the present time gives the board power, if they have the land and the money, to transfer these soldier settlers from one place to another. The question I desire to ask is this: will the government place in the estimates a sufficient sum to permit the settlers to be moved from places where the land is of no agricultural value to other districts where they can make a living?
Mr. "FORKE: I am afraid that is a matter of government policy. I could not make a promise of that kind.
Will the minister lay it before the cabinet?
Yes.
Preamble agreed to.

I made a suggestion which was not opposed by anybody, and I think it is in the interests of a large number of soldiers, namely, that paragraph (j) should be amended to read, "who is desirous of repurchasing the land," instead of "who is desirous of returning to the land," so that it

That is all right, I accept that amendment.
